reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / vascular medicine consensus documents
clinicalPearls: Non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arteriopathy that predominantly affects women
Most commonly involves the renal and internal carotid or vertebral arteries
The multifocal medial subtype produces the classic angiographic string-of-beads appearance
Renal involvement typically presents with early-onset or resistant hypertension
Cervical involvement may cause headache, pulsatile tinnitus, cervical bruit, dissection, or stroke
Screening for aneurysms elsewhere, including intracranial aneurysms, is recommended once diagnosed
Management includes antiplatelet therapy, blood pressure control, and angioplasty for significant renal stenosis
reference.pathophysiology: Fibromuscular dysplasia is an idiopathic, segmental, non-inflammatory and non-atherosclerotic disorder of medium-sized arteries. Abnormal proliferation and disorganised deposition of collagen and fibrous tissue within the arterial wall, most often the media, create alternating areas of stenosis and mural dilatation that give the beaded angiographic pattern; focal forms produce discrete stenoses. The disordered wall architecture predisposes to dissection, aneurysm formation, and thromboembolism, so cerebrovascular events may arise from stenosis, dissection, or embolism rather than from atherosclerotic plaque.
additionalDifferentials: Vasculitis such as Takayasu or polyarteritis nodosa
Ehlers-Danlos and other connective tissue arteriopathies
Spontaneous cervical artery dissection from other causes
Standing arterial spasm or reversible vasoconstriction
additionalInvestigations: Catheter angiography or CT and MR angiography showing the string-of-beads or focal stenosis
Duplex ultrasound of renal and cervical arteries for screening and follow-up
Intracranial vascular imaging to detect associated aneurysms
Blood pressure evaluation and assessment of renovascular hypertension
Whole-arterial-bed imaging because the disease is frequently multifocal
redFlags: Arterial dissection presenting with neck pain, Horner syndrome, or stroke
Rupture of an associated intracranial aneurysm
Accelerated or resistant hypertension from renal artery involvement
Recurrent transient ischaemic attacks or infarction
reference.prognosis: Many patients have a benign course, but complications such as dissection, aneurysm rupture, and stroke can be serious; renal disease often responds well to angioplasty, and overall outlook depends on the vascular beds involved.
pitfalls: Assuming stenosis is atherosclerotic in a young patient and missing the diagnosis
Failing to screen for intracranial and other aneurysms after diagnosis
Overlooking arterial dissection as the cause of a stroke in cervical FMD
Not imaging additional arterial beds given the multifocal nature of the disease
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
